Unit 1 • SL

Computational Thinking

Introduction

How do we take a messy, real-world problem and turn it into something a computer can solve?

This unit introduces Computational Thinking — a powerful problem-solving toolkit used by computer scientists. You'll learn to transform "wicked" messy problems into clear, structured solutions.

The journey goes like this: start with a real-world problem, create a problem specification to define what you're solving, apply the four pillars of computational thinking to analyse it, then design an algorithm and represent it visually as a flowchart.

The Four Pillars of Computational Thinking

Computational thinking is a toolkit of techniques for problem-solving. It's not about thinking like a computer — it's about thinking like a computer scientist.

🔍 Abstraction

Removing unnecessary detail to focus on what matters. Like the London Tube Map — it ignores real geography to show connections clearly.

🧩 Decomposition

Breaking a complex problem into smaller, manageable parts. This supports modularity and allows multiple people to work on different parts.

🔄 Pattern Recognition

Identifying similarities in problems. This simplifies solutions by reusing code and developing functions that can be applied multiple times.

📋 Algorithmic Thinking

Designing step-by-step instructions that are specific, clear, and in the right order. Every step must be unambiguous.

Common Mistake

Students often define "decomposition" as breaking down a program into smaller sub-programs. This isn't accurate — at the stage decomposition occurs, there is no program yet. You break down the problem, not the code.

Problem Specification

Before writing any code, you must truly understand the problem. A problem specification is a formal document that defines:

  • Stakeholders — Who is affected by or interested in this problem?
  • Problem Statement — What exactly are we trying to solve?
  • Inputs & Outputs — What data goes in? What results come out?
  • Constraints — What limitations or boundaries exist?
  • Success Criteria — How will we know if our solution works?

Flowcharts & Trace Tables

Flowcharts are diagrams used to design and describe algorithms visually. They use standard symbols connected by flowlines to show the execution flow.

SymbolNamePurpose
⬭TerminatorStart or end of the process
▱Input/OutputInput or output of data
▭ProcessAction, calculation, or assignment
◇DecisionYes/No or True/False branching
→FlowlineDirection of data flow

A trace table (or "dry run") tracks how variables change as you step through an algorithm. It's used to verify your algorithm produces the expected output.

Don't Forget

Always label decision branches with Yes/No or True/False. Never leave flowlines disconnected — every path must lead somewhere.

Key Terminology
TermDefinition
AlgorithmA finite sequence of instructions that needs to be followed step-by-step to solve a problem.
AbstractionRemoving unnecessary detail to focus on the essential aspects of a problem.
DecompositionBreaking down complex problems into smaller, more manageable parts.
Pattern RecognitionIdentifying similarities in the details of problems to reuse solutions.
Problem SpecificationA formal document defining stakeholders, inputs, outputs, constraints, and success criteria.
StakeholderA person or group with an interest in or affected by the problem.
ConstraintsLimitations or boundaries that the solution must work within.
FlowchartA diagram using standard symbols to represent an algorithm visually.
Trace TableA table used to track variable changes when stepping through an algorithm.
Dry RunManually executing an algorithm step-by-step to verify its correctness.

Think Deeper

"The map is not the territory." When we abstract, we create a simplified model. What do we gain from this simplification? What might we lose?
